slides.text: Recurrent neural networks suffer from vanishing gradients because the weight matrix \(W\) is multiplied at each time step, making it impossible to retain long-term memory.
The basic idea for a solution to vanishing gradients had already appeared in ResNet: provide a “constant error carousel”, a shortcut for the gradients.
The constant error carousel idea led to a more complex recurrent unit that explicitly controls memory: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM).
LSTM was introduced by Hochreiter & Schmidhuber in 1995 and 1997.
The modern form of LSTM was introduced by Gers & Schmidhuber in 2000.
The LSTM cell maintains a cell state \(c_t\) and a hidden state \(h_t\).
Three gates—input, forget, and output—regulate information flow in the LSTM cell.
The candidate cell state is \(c'_t = \tanh(W_{xc} x_t + W_{hc} h_{t-1} + b_{c'})\).
The input gate is \(i_t = \sigma(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + b_i)\).
The forget gate is \(f_t = \sigma(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + b_f)\).
The output gate is \(o_t = \sigma(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + b_o)\).
The cell state is \(c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t\).
The hidden state (block output) is \(h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)\).
If the forget gate is fully open (\(f_t = 1\)), then the cell state becomes \(c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t\).
Consequently, when \(f_t = 1\), the gradient \(\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} = 1\), allowing gradients to flow unchanged.
One problem with the basic LSTM is that the gates only see the hidden state \(h_{t-1} = o_{t-1} \odot \tanh(c_{t-1})\).
If the output gate is closed, the LSTM’s behavior becomes independent of the cell state.
This problem is remedied by adding peephole connections, which are extra weight matrices that give the gates direct access to \(c_{t-1}\).
With peephole connections, the input gate becomes \(i_t = \sigma(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + W_{pi} c_{t-1} + b_i)\).
With peephole connections, the forget gate becomes \(f_t = \sigma(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + W_{pf} c_{t-1} + b_f)\).
With peephole connections, the output gate becomes \(o_t = \sigma(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + W_{po} c_{t-1} + b_o)\).
A huge number of LSTM variations exist—any gate can be removed, peepholes can be added or omitted, activation functions altered, etc.
Greff et al. (2015) experimentally compared many LSTM variants and found that some significantly simpler architectures with one fewer gate performed nearly as well as vanilla LSTM.
Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) were introduced by Cho et al. in 2014.
GRU implements the constant error carousel but with a simpler design than LSTM.
The GRU merges cell state and hidden state into a single vector \(h_t\).
GRU uses only two gates: update gate and reset gate.
The GRU update gate is \(u_t = \sigma(W_{xu} x_t + W_{hu} h_{t-1} + b_u)\).
The GRU reset gate is \(r_t = \sigma(W_{xr} x_t + W_{hr} h_{t-1} + b_r)\).
The GRU candidate state is \(h'_t = \tanh(W_{xh'} x_t + W_{hh'} (r_t \odot h_{t-1}))\).
The GRU state update is \(h_t = (1 - u_t) \odot h'_t + u_t \odot h_{t-1}\).
GRU has 6 weight matrices, while basic LSTM has 8 and LSTM with peepholes has 11.
GRU has fewer parameters than LSTM.
GRU is only slightly worse in performance than LSTM.
For a fixed computational budget, one can use more GRU units than LSTM units and obtain better networks.
Józefowicz et al. (2015) conducted a huge experimental comparison of GRU variations with an evolutionary approach and identified three particularly interesting architectures.
Attention is in large part the interaction with working memory (Knudsen, 2007).
In human vision, the fovea is very small, so we only perceive a tiny high-resolution patch at any moment.
The human eyes move in rapid saccades, sequentially fixating on different parts of the scene.
The process of saccades can be both conscious and unconscious.

The Invisible Gorilla experiment (Simons & Chabris, 1999) is a famous illustration of attention: observers concentrating on a ball-passing task completely miss a person in a gorilla suit walking through the frame.
A neural network might benefit from consciously deciding “what to look at”.
One of the first works on foveal glimpses was by Larochelle & Hinton (2010), which modelled the positions of saccades and learned a sequence of glimpses.
The idea of foveal glimpses was fully realized in “Recurrent Models of Visual Attention” by Mnih et al. in 2014.
In Recurrent Models of Visual Attention, at each time step, the network receives a glimpse \(g_t\) computed as \(g_t = f_g(x_t, l_{t-1}; \theta_g)\).
The network updates its hidden state via \(h_t = f_h(h_{t-1}, g_t; \theta_h)\).
The network outputs a new location \(l_t\) sampled from \(p(\cdot \mid f_l(h_t; \theta_l))\).
The network outputs an action \(a_t\) sampled from \(p(\cdot \mid f_a(h_t; \theta_a))\).
A reward \(r_t\) is received after the action, with the goal of correct final classification.
The model defines a stochastic policy \(\pi((l_t,a_t)\mid s_{1:t};\theta)\) implemented by an RNN.
The objective is to maximize the expected total reward \(J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p(s_{1:T};\theta)}[R] = \mathbb{E}_{p(s_{1:T};\theta)}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T r_t\right]\).
This is a reinforcement learning problem, which can be optimized using the REINFORCE algorithm and other policy gradient methods.
The figures in the original paper show attention trajectories walking around an image, focusing on the relevant object.
Ba et al. (2015) extended the recurrent visual attention approach to deep models trained with variational approximations.
Gregor et al. (2015) proposed DRAW, a recurrent attention-based variational autoencoder for image generation.
Machine translation is a canonical sequence-to-sequence problem.
An RNN language model factors a sequence \(X = (x_1,\dots,x_T)\) as \(p(X) = p(x_1) p(x_2 \mid x_1) \cdots p(x_T \mid x_{<T})\).
For translation, one can use an encoder-decoder architecture (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014).
In an encoder-decoder architecture, an RNN encoder compresses the source sentence into a fixed-size vector.
An RNN decoder generates the target sentence from that fixed-size vector.
The critical limitation of the encoder-decoder architecture is that everything must be squeezed through a single fixed-size vector, causing performance degradation on long sequences.
The solution to the fixed-size bottleneck is to let the decoder attend to all encoder hidden states, weighted by relevance.
Bahdanau et al. (2014) combined a bidirectional LSTM encoder with an attention mechanism.
In soft attention (Luong et al., 2015a,b; Jean et al., 2015), the attention score \(e_{tj}\) is computed as a function \(a(z_{t-1}, j)\).
The attention weights \(\alpha_{tj}\) are obtained by applying softmax to the scores: \(\alpha_{tj} = \operatorname{softmax}(e_{tj})\).
c_t = \sum_j \alpha_{tj} h_j
The decoder state is updated as z_t = f(s_{t-1}, y_{t-1}, c_t)
Visualisations of the attention weights show clear word alignments
Visualisations of the attention weights show much better target word order
Vinyals et al. (2015) applied the same attention idea to parsing
Vinyals et al. (2015) treated parsing as "Grammar as a Foreign Language"
Wu et al. (2016) scaled the architecture to very deep stacks: 8 encoder layers and 8 decoder layers of LSTMs
The paper by Wu et al. (2016) is titled "Google’s Neural Machine Translation System: Bridging the Gap between Human and Machine Translation"
Stacked LSTMs stop working beyond 4–5 layers
The authors added residual connections to the stacked LSTMs
Residual connections are like ResNet
The bottom layer of the encoder is bidirectional
This system powered Google Translate for several years
Show and Tell (Vinyals et al., 2015) used a CNN to extract a fixed image feature vector
The LSTM decoder generated a caption word by word
The model maximised \sum_{(I,S)} \log p(S \mid I; \theta)
Show and Tell worked reasonably well
Show and Tell lacked fine-grained alignment
Show, Attend and Tell (Xu et al., 2015) introduced spatial attention over CNN feature vectors {a_i}
At each step, a context vector is formed as \phi(\{a_i\},\{\alpha_{t,i}\}) = \sum_{i=1}^L \alpha_{t,i} a_i
Two variants of attention were studied
Soft attention is a deterministic weighted sum
Soft attention is differentiable and trained end-to-end
Hard attention is stochastic
Hard attention is trained by maximising a variational lower bound
L_s = \sum_s p(s \mid a) \log p(y \mid s, a)
L_s \leq \log \sum_s p(s \mid a) p(y \mid s, a)
The right-hand side equals \log p(y \mid a)

The gradient is \frac{\partial L_s}{\partial W} = \sum_s p(s \mid a) \!\left[ \frac{\partial \log p(y \mid s, a)}{\partial W} + \log p(y \mid s, a) \frac{\partial \log p(s \mid a)}{\partial W} \right]
The expectation is approximated by sampling s from the attention distribution \alpha_i
Figures demonstrate generated captions with both hard and soft attention
Figures highlight the attended regions
Failures can be analysed by inspecting attention
The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) abandons recurrence entirely
The Transformer uses only attention
The Transformer architecture follows the encoder-decoder pattern
Each encoder block consists of a self-attention layer followed by a position-wise feedforward network
The decoder adds masked self-attention
The decoder adds encoder-decoder attention
Because all tokens are processed in parallel, training is orders of magnitude faster than with RNNs
Self-attention is inspired by information retrieval
An input sequence of vectors X in R^{d × L} is transformed into queries Q = W_Q X
Keys K = W_K X
Values V = W_V X
W_Q and W_K are in R^{q × d}
W_V is in R^{v × d}
Usually v = q
The attention scores are scaled dot-products: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(\frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} Q K^T) V
Scaling by 1/\sqrt{q} prevents extremely small gradients
The output is an L × v matrix
A single attention head only captures one type of relationship
To enrich the representation, the Transformer uses multi-head attention
Multi-head attention uses H different sets of weight matrices
The H sets produce H independent outputs Z^1,...,Z^H
The outputs are concatenated into Z_concat in R^{L × Hv}
The concatenated output is projected back to dimension d: Z = (Z_concat W_O)^T
W_O is in R^{Hv × d}
Multi-head attention allows the layer to mix information from different representation subspaces
The decoder generates tokens autoregressively
The decoder must not attend to future positions
Masked self-attention sets the pre-softmax values for future tokens to -∞
Setting pre-softmax values to -∞ forces their attention weights to zero
Encoder-decoder attention uses the same attention mechanism
In encoder-decoder attention, queries come from the previous decoder layer
Queries are the partially generated output
In encoder-decoder attention, keys and values come from the encoder's final layer
The decoder performs "retrieval" over the encoder's output, conditioned on the tokens already produced
Transformers use subword tokenization
The most common subword tokenization is Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)
BPE starts from vocabulary counts: {cat:10, pet:12, mat:5, rat:8, eats:4}
The text is split into characters: {c:10, a:27, t:39, p:12, e:16, m:5, r:8, s:4}
Character pairs are counted: {ca:10, at:27, pe:12, et:12, ma:5, ra:8, ea:4, ts:4}
The most frequent pair "at" (frequency 27) is replaced by a new symbol Z
After replacement, the vocabulary becomes {cZ:10, pet:12, mZ:5, rZ:8, eZs:4}
The process is repeated (next replacing "pe" or "et" with Y) until the desired vocabulary size is reached
BPE efficiently handles rare words by encoding frequent subword units
Self-attention is completely invariant to token order
To inject sequence information, the Transformer adds positional encodings to the input embeddings
Positional encodings use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies
PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d})
PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d})
pos is the token position
d is the embedding dimension
This positional encoding scheme allows the model to extrapolate to longer sequences than seen during training
Relative distances can be inferred from phase differences
The Transformer trains 100× faster than comparable recurrent models
The Transformer achieves superior translation quality
Self-attention drastically shortens the path length between any two positions
This facilitates long-range dependencies
The attention weights offer a degree of interpretability
One can visualise which tokens the model is attending to at each layer
Figures show example attention weight matrices, revealing syntactic and semantic relations

transcript.text: Transformers transformed deep learning a decade ago.
The main problems of recurrent networks are exactly the same as the problems of deep networks in general, like convolutional networks.
The problem is signal saturation.
As you go through layers, signal is lost when some layers saturate.
Especially as gradients flow back, signal is lost when some layers saturate.
When a layer stops training, its derivatives become zero.
Multiplying by zero prevents anything below from training.
An RNN is in effect a very deep network.
When processing an input, activations pass through as many trainable neural layers as there are elements in the sequence.
Any recurrent network is, by default, as deep as the input sequence.
Usually the input sequence is very deep.
When people speak of "deep" RNNs, they mean several layers of recurrent processing.
Even a single-layer RNN is a very deep network in the computational graph.
The vanishing-gradient problem is essentially the same as signal saturation.
As you go backward with gradients, you keep multiplying by the same weight matrix $W$.
All cells share $W$, which makes the vanishing-gradient problem worse.
If $W$ has spectral radius less than 1, repeatedly multiplying by a number less than 1 shrinks the gradients to zero.
You will not notice the vanishing-gradient problem from the loss curve.
Exploding gradients cause obvious numerical overflows and breakdowns.
Vanishing gradients do not cause obvious breakdowns.
Even if gradients become exactly zero after a few steps back from the loss, $W$ still trains because it participates in the last cells.
The weight gradients look fine.
But the network is now making decisions based only on the last few elements of the sequence.
It cannot carry $x_1$ to influence the output at step $t$.
The network loses long-term memory.
The solution to the vanishing-gradient problem in RNNs is to add residual connections.
Recurrent networks pioneered the use of residual connections because they do not work without it.
The idea of residual connections in RNNs originated in Jürgen Schmidhuber's group in the 1990s.
The idea was later applied to deep feed-forward networks around 2015.
The key is a highway for gradients that avoids direct multiplication by weight matrices that could vanish.
This leads to the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM).
In an LSTM cell, the hidden state is artificially split into two parts.
One part, $C$, is the long-term memory.
The long-term memory stays on the highway.
We read from and write to $C$.
$C$ is not repeatedly multiplied by weight matrices.
$C$ is like the residual path around layers.
The other part, $h_t$, is the ordinary hidden state that participates in the cell's operations.
The cell outputs the next $C$ and $h$.
Input $x_t$ also enters the LSTM cell.
The LSTM is built from gates.
Gates are a concept now common in many architectures.
A gate takes two inputs $x$ and $y$.
The gate multiplies each input by a weight matrix.
The gate adds the results (plus a bias).
The gate passes the sum through an activation function $f$.
The output is $f(W_x x + W_y y)$.
The bias is not drawn in diagrams.
The first gate in the LSTM is the forget gate.
The forget gate receives $h$ with weight matrix $W_{hf}$.
The forget gate receives $x$ with weight matrix $W_{xf}$.
You multiply $C_t$ by the output of the forget gate, component-wise.
The output vector is called $F_t$.
The forget gate takes a linear combination of $H$ and $X$.
The forget gate passes the linear combination through the logistic sigmoid $\sigma$.
The sigmoid produces a vector of values strictly between 0 and 1.
Multiplying component-wise by the memory cell gives the intuition of erasing things from memory.
If the forget gate output is close to 1, the cell is retained.
If the forget gate output is close to 0, the cell is erased.
Gating works by a small part of the network producing a control vector that controls other parts, not additional data.
The meaning of $F_t$ is which memory cells to erase.
You cannot use real logic gates because they are piecewise constant and gradients wouldn't flow.
A continuous approximation works.
The candidate cell state $\tilde{C}_t$ produces the new numbers to write to memory.
The candidate cell state is computed from the same inputs $H$ and $X$.
The candidate cell state uses its own weight matrices.
The candidate cell state uses a hyperbolic tangent (tanh) activation, not a sigmoid.
The tanh is not set in stone and can be modified.
The input gate is another sigmoid gate.
The input gate decides which parts of $\tilde{C}_t$ to write into memory.
To write, you multiply $\tilde{C}_t$ component-wise by the input gate's output, and add the result to memory.
Writing to memory means addition.
After erasing by multiplying $C_t$ by something near zero, adding the gated candidate writes the new value into that cell.
The only remaining part is to define $H$ for the next step.
$H$ is produced from the long-term memory $C_t$.
$H$ is essentially a copy of $C_t$, but passed through a hyperbolic tangent.
An output gate with a sigmoid controls which parts of $C_t$ are read into $H_t$.
This control is via component-wise multiplication.
The LSTM cell is a program for memory manipulation.
In the LSTM, you can erase, write, and decide what to write.
The candidate cell state enables deciding what to write.
The beauty of the LSTM is the straight highway for gradients to flow through.
The highway is interrupted only when memory is intentionally erased.
The LSTM has many weights: eight matrices.
Half of the eight matrices are of size $d \times d$.
Half of the eight matrices are of size $d \times d'$.
$d$ is the size of $h$ and $c$.
$d$ is typically at least 256, sometimes up to 1000.
$d'$ is the input representation size.
These large weight matrices made LSTMs difficult to train initially.
Despite training difficulty, LSTMs performed well on toy problems.
The LSTM was extremely successful.
The LSTM dates from around 1995-2000.
The version with all these gates appeared in Schmidhuber's group by 2000.
The LSTM just works.
Even today, when building a recurrent network, you will use LSTMs.
The LSTM is the most important recurrent construction.
The LSTM provides that uninterrupted gradient highway.
Training huge LSTMs became feasible only around 2015.
Since then, big LSTMs have been the standard for large recurrent networks.
AlphaStar, the StarCraft-playing network, used LSTMs.
The LSTM architecture was the first successful attempt at memory manipulation.
The LSTM was introduced 25 years ago.
The LSTM still stands unsurpassed.
Many attempts have been made to improve the LSTM.
The LSTM cell in its modern form (2000) contains a forget gate, input gate, candidate cell state, and output gate.
One early modification added peepholes.
Originally, the gates had no access to the memory state $C$.
Without access, one could not see what was being erased.
Peephole connections provided extra inputs from $C$.
Peephole connections increased the number of weight matrices.
Later efforts tried to simplify the LSTM by removing some gates.
The paper "LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey" found that on some problems an entire gate could be removed with little effect.
The broader goal remained to achieve a memory highway for gradient flow while making the cell more efficient.
This led to the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU).
The GRU was developed in 2014.
The GRU is similar to the LSTM.
The GRU uses far fewer matrices than the LSTM.
The GRU does not separate the cell state $C$ and hidden state $H$.
In the GRU, there is only one hidden state.
Instead of separately erasing and writing, the GRU uses an update gate $U$.
The update gate $U$ uses a sigmoid ($\sigma$) output.
The update gate forms a convex combination: the new state is $U \cdot H_{\text{old}} + (1-U) \cdot H'$.
$H'$ is the candidate state.
This merges erasing and writing into a single gate.
This saves weight matrices.
In place of the output gate, the GRU has a reset gate.
The reset gate selects which parts of the memory feed into the candidate state $H'$.
The GRU uses only six weight matrices instead of eight (or eleven with peepholes).
The GRU appears to do the same job more efficiently than the LSTM.
In 2015-2016, GRUs were widely adopted in natural language processing.
For reasons that remain theoretically unclear, the field later switched back to LSTMs.
Recent large-scale recurrent models, like AlphaStar (around 2020), are more likely to be LSTMs.
Schmidhuber's original construction seems empirically better.
The decision between LSTM and GRU is based on practical performance.
Why the LSTM architecture is superior is unknown.
The longevity of the LSTM is remarkable.
Throughout deep learning history, neural architecture search and massive compute have yielded improvements (e.g., EfficientNet, Swish).
Analogous efforts on recurrent cells have not produced a lasting replacement.
Google published a paper introducing a cell with only four weight matrices.
This cell is similar to a GRU but even more efficient.
These cells are virtually unused.
They likely work well on the test datasets where they were developed.
They do not generalize.
The LSTM remains the best general-purpose recurrent unit.
The classic LSTM benchmark from Hochreiter and Schmidhuber provides an input with two channels.
One channel is a stream of random numbers between 0 and 1.
The other channel is a stream of zeros with exactly two ones, acting as markers.
The task is to output the sum of the two random numbers that correspond to the marked positions.
This is an ideal toy test for memory.
The network must store the first marked value and later add the second.
LSTMs and GRUs both handle the benchmark problem well.
Because the problem is simple, GRUs excel.
A simple linear RNN fails to learn the benchmark.
On the classic LSTM benchmark, an LSTM eventually starts learning but has not fully trained after 600 iterations.
On the classic LSTM benchmark, a GRU learns much faster and from an earlier point.
Plots like this once convinced the community that GRUs were superior.
This benchmark is a very easy problem.
A more efficient cell wins on easy tasks but likely does not scale to truly hard ones.
In the summing problem, when the LSTM sees a marker, the write gate spikes.
This writes a large value to the cell.
At other times, the LSTM writes little.
The cell state jumps to the correct sum.
The running guess tracks the true sum exactly.
Straightforward recurrent networks without gating cannot solve the summing problem.
They lack the long-term memory to recall a number from many steps ago and add it to the current input.
That is the core idea behind all gated recurrent cells.
It is remarkably unclear how attention is supposed to function.
Our brain seems to work very differently in this regard from the artificial neural networks seen so far.
When looking at an image, the visual cortex processes images somewhat like convolutional networks.
The visual cortex extracts local features, then combines them into global, semantically richer features.
When looking at an image, your field of vision is much wider than the object of focus.
If something happens outside the focus while concentrating, you will likely miss it.
This happens even though it is still in your field of view.
Mapping this attentional behavior to standard neural networks is strange.
A convolution over an image extracts features from every part of the image.
These features are then combined into more global representations.
A convolutional network cannot simply miss a cat in an image.
Humans can miss a cat in an image.
The difference is an attention mechanism.
Alexander Luria was a neuropsychologist.
Alexander Luria was a prominent international figure in the 1930s and 1940s.
Alexander Luria posited that the three main pillars of neuropsychology are attention, memory, and cognition.
Since Luria, we have come to understand that in the brain attention operates largely through memory.
There is a very short-term working memory that stores just a few recent items.
Even a person not paying attention can usually recite the last few words they heard.
A person not paying attention cannot recite words from thirty seconds earlier.
Working memory acts as a buffer into which most recent events go.
A filter selects which parts of the buffer are important for further processing.
Information gets lost at the filter step.
While focused on counting passes in the basketball video, many viewers completely miss a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene.
Even when looking directly at something, you may not process it.
Our visual system does not process the entire field of view in high resolution.
Only a small central region, the fovea, provides sharp detail.
Peripheral vision is blurry.
We do not notice the blurriness of peripheral vision because our gaze constantly shifts in saccadic motions.
Gaze shifts sample different snippets.
The brain assembles the snippets into a coherent picture.
The original motivation for incorporating attention mechanisms into deep learning was to emulate the selective processing of the human visual system.
This emulation simulates the blurriness of peripheral vision to focus on salient parts.
Our eyes evolved under metabolic and structural constraints.
The original motivation for attention was to save weights and input size, making processing more efficient.
If you look at a few small snippets of a large image, you use only the pixels from those parts.
With attention, the rest of the image can be blurrier, meaning fewer pixels are used.
By using fewer pixels, the input size becomes much smaller.
With three glimpses, each on a small part, the total input size is much smaller.
In addition to recognizing from blurred images, you also need to choose where to look (the glimpse positions).
The glimpse positions form a sequence.
The next glimpse can depend on what was seen in the previous one.
Early models of attention were recurrent.
This gave rise to the field of recurrent visual attention.
Recurrent visual attention is now outdated.
The goal of recurrent visual attention was to walk around a relatively big picture, choose where to look while blurring the rest.
This approach enabled more accurate and efficient processing with a recurrent mechanism for selecting glimpses.
Machine translation is a problem well-suited for recurrent encoder-decoder architectures.
In a recurrent encoder-decoder for machine translation, the encoder reads the input and produces a hidden state.
The last hidden state gives an intermediate representation vector z of the input sentence.
The decoder takes z and decodes it into the output sequence.
In practice, the decoder has a hidden state h' and z is the input to every decoder cell.
When LSTM/GRU architectures were applied to machine translation, they encountered an unsolvable scalability problem.
This architecture achieved state-of-the-art around 2014.
The architecture works well for short sentences like "hello world".
The problem is the dimension of the intermediate representation Z.
You cannot find a good dimension for Z: it is either too small or too big.
If Z is too small, training converges easily, but it cannot pack enough meaning.
With a small Z, the model works for short sentences but fails on longer sentences.
If Z is made longer, training becomes harder.
A very long Z means the hidden states and decoder inputs become longer, leading to quadratically more weights.
With very long Z, you lack sufficient data and compute to train the model.
So you can either have a small Z with good training but no scalability, or a large Z with impossible training.
Plotting quality against sequence length shows very good quality for short sentences, then a sharp drop.
One would want quality to drop gracefully and still work for longer sequences.
Attention mechanisms for encoder-decoder recurrent networks were introduced to fix this scalability problem.
The concept of attention for encoder-decoder architectures remains important today.
The problem with Z is that it is only one vector for the entire input.
In transformers, there is also not a single vector for the whole sequence.
When translating specific words, the corresponding source word should be more important at that step than other input words.
A single vector has no way to express dynamic importance; you must cram everything into one vector.
The first step to fix this is to remove the assumption that everything must be in a single vector.
In an encoder-decoder with attention, the encoder processes the input and produces a vector for each input token.
The encoder can be a bidirectional recurrent network.
To get the vector for each token, you take the two hidden states (forward and backward) and push them through a feedforward layer.
You cannot simply concatenate all token vectors and feed them to the decoder; that would cause the "Z too long" problem.
At each step of the decoder, you want a single vector of a manageable size.
The attention mechanism combines the token vectors into a single vector for the decoder.
At decoder step t, indicated by decoder hidden state h'_t, a small attention network is used.
The attention network receives an encoder output z_i and the current decoder hidden state h'_t.
The attention network outputs a score a_i that indicates the importance of that input token at that decoding step.
A score a_i is computed for every encoder output z_i.
The scores are converted into a probability distribution via softmax, giving coefficients α_i.
The softmax output is a convex combination that sums to 1.
The resulting context vector U_t (or Z_t) is the input for the decoder at time step t.
The context vector is a linear combination of all encoder token representations.
The weights of the linear combination are determined by a separate attention network.
The attention weights express which source tokens are being translated at the current step.
For example, when producing the third word, attention should focus on the source word "world", giving it a high weight.
There is no explicit training signal for the attention mechanism.
The training dataset consists only of sentence pairs (e.g., English–Russian translations).
We never label which source token corresponds to which target token.
The attention network is a small component, about 2% of the total weights.
The attention network is trained end-to-end from the translation objective.
This small attention component drives the results, accounting for the difference between red and purple performance curves.
The attention network learns to find the correct tokens and produce the appropriate weights just from the overall loss.

A general principle in deep learning is that if you structurally give the network the capacity to do a desired job, even without separate supervision for that sub-component, it often learns to do it correctly by optimizing the overall task.
In late 2014, Bahdanau et al. introduced this attention mechanism for encoder-decoder architectures.
The mechanism indeed trained to align words.
Attention weights are easy to interpret.
In French-to-English translation, the attention alignment matrix is mostly diagonal when word order matches.
The alignment matrix shows off-diagonal weights where languages differ in word order.
For example, French "la destruction" becomes English "destruction" with high attention on both French source words.
French "arme chimique" becomes English "chemical weapons" with swapped order, and the attention weights reflect this.
A simple recurrent network with attention can learn to reverse an input sequence by attending to the reverse diagonal.
Without attention, the network would need to memorize the whole sequence in a fixed-size context vector, which fails for long sequences.
A network can learn to sort numbers: at each step, the attention weights focus on the current t-th smallest value.
Attention enables handling outputs with complex structure, such as syntax trees, by linearizing them as strings and treating the problem as a translation.
In 2016, a Google paper described their neural machine translation system that worked in this same way (encoder-decoder with attention).
Google's earlier translation system was an encoder-decoder with attention.
After Google switched to this architecture around 2015–2016, Google Translate became much better.
Before 2016, Google Translate was ineffective for translating research papers from Russian to English; fixing its output took more time than translating from scratch.
In 2015–2016, a phase transition occurred where it became more efficient to use Google Translate and then fix mistakes than to translate manually.
This was when machine translation started doing useful work.
You can have an encoder-decoder where input and output have different modalities and different networks.
The image captioning problem in 2015 used an encoder-decoder with a GoogLeNet encoder and an LSTM decoder.
Adding attention made the image captioning system much better.
Attention can highlight specific parts of the input even when the input is not text or a sequence.
With a picture, we take a CNN and stop it early to retain spatial geometry instead of compressing into a single feature vector.
For a 256×256 input, we might stop at a 14×14 feature map, giving 196 feature vectors.
An attention network learns coefficients to combine these 196 feature vectors.
This attention mechanism is interpretable: you can see where the network is looking as it generates each word.

When generating "a woman is throwing a frisbee in the park", the attention focuses on the people for "woman", on the throwing action for "throwing", on the frisbee for "frisbee", and on the background for "park".
Transformers appeared in 2017.
The paper "Attention Is All You Need" introduced the transformer in 2017.
The authors of the paper "Attention Is All You Need" likely did not fully realize the impact of their work.
The paper "Attention Is All You Need" was not very ambitious.
The paper "Attention Is All You Need" proposed a different, more efficient way of doing roughly the same thing with similar results.
Since the paper's publication, the whole field of machine learning switched to transformers.
Much of the rest of this class will build on transformers.
Two key qualities of transformers emerged after the original experiments: extreme generality and exceptional scalability.
Transformers proved extremely general.
Transformers are very good at noticing internal correlations within complicated data.
Transformers work on sequences of vectors regardless of where those vectors come from — text, images, etc.
Transformers are exceptionally scalable.
You can scale transformers up, add more parameters, and performance keeps improving without saturating.
Modern large language models have gone from tens of millions to hundreds of billions to now trillions of parameters.
As large language models scale up, their performance keeps improving.
This kind of unbounded scaling had never happened before transformers.
LSTMs couldn't be scaled the same way — either complexity grew too fast or they saturated.
The basic structure of the transformer is very similar to the recurrent encoder-decoder with attention discussed earlier.
The main new element in transformers is the self-attention mechanism.
The original transformer is an encoder-decoder architecture for machine translation.
The encoder consists of six identical layers.
The decoder also has six identical layers.
The encoder receives text in one language.
The decoder produces text in another language.
The input to the transformer encoder is not raw tokens but continuous vectors called embeddings.
In NLP, it was common to convert one-hot representations of words or tokens into continuous vectors called embeddings.
It is standard practice to convert a large vocabulary of discrete items into dense vectors.
The embeddings in the transformer are a matrix of vectors trained along with the rest of the network.
For every input token, a vector is looked up from the embedding matrix and placed instead of the token.
After the embedding layer, the input sequence becomes a sequence of vectors.
The entire transformer simply rewrites sequences of vectors into sequences of vectors.
Every encoder layer takes a sequence of vectors as input and produces a sequence of the same size.
The representations are rewritten multiple times (six times in the original transformer).
By the top encoder layer, the vector for each token is a semantically rich representation of that token in the context of all other tokens.
The decoder is an autoregressive language model.
The decoder produces output tokens one by one, taking as input the history of what it has already written and outputting the next token.
You must run the transformer decoder as many times as there are tokens to produce.
Speculative decoding and similar techniques work around this sequential restriction, but by default the decoder is autoregressive.
The encoder output is used in the decoder at every layer on every step.
Inside an encoder layer: a self-attention layer, then layer normalization, then a feed-forward (fully connected) layer, then another layer normalization.
A residual connection goes around the self-attention and meets the layer normalization.
Layer normalization is a normalization technique applied across the outputs of the current layer, unlike batch normalization which normalizes across the mini-batch.
Transformers are large and often only one instance fits in memory, making batch normalization impractical.
Layer normalization is used to average out gradients, keep the loss landscape smooth, and control the absolute values of outputs.
The feed-forward layer in a transformer is very important and accounts for a large fraction of the total weights.
The feed-forward layer mixes the features within each vector separately.
The decoder layer contains self-attention (masked), a feed-forward layer, and layer norms, plus one extra encoder-decoder attention layer.
The encoder output vectors go into the encoder-decoder attention layer.
After the decoder, a linear layer followed by a softmax produces probabilities for the next token.
The softmax at the end is essentially logistic regression.
Self-attention is motivated by neural information retrieval.
In neural information retrieval, queries and documents are processed by separate encoders to produce vectors in a common latent space.
The encoders can be different, but they map both queries and documents to the same space.
The retrieval system is trained so that the representations of relevant documents are close to the representation of the query.
The similarity between a query and a document can be measured by the dot product of their vectors.
After training, retrieval becomes a nearest-neighbor search in this latent space.
Self-attention applies this query-document idea to the same set of vectors, which serve as both queries and documents.
Every transformer layer receives a sequence of vectors as input: $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$.
To create a query, the vector $x_1$ is multiplied by a matrix $W^Q$ to obtain the first query vector $q_1$.
To create keys, all vectors $x_i$ are multiplied by $W^K$ to get key vectors $k_1, k_2, \dots, k_n$.
The central idea is that queries and keys live in the same latent space, so similarity is measured with a dot product.
This similarity becomes the attention score.
From $x_1$'s query and all keys, affinities are computed as $a_{1i} = q_1 \cdot k_i$.
The affinities are rescaled by $1/\sqrt{d}$ and softmax is applied to obtain attention weights $\alpha_{1i}$ that sum to 1.
All $x_i$ are multiplied by a third matrix $W^V$ to produce value vectors $v_i$.
The output for the first position is $z_1 = \sum_i \alpha_{1i} v_i$.
This process is repeated for each position $j$: compute $q_j$, use the same keys and softmax to get $\alpha_{ji}$, then $z_j = \sum_i \alpha_{ji} v_i$.
In practice, self-attention is computed in matrix form.
The matrices of queries, keys, and values are computed as $Q = X W^Q$, $K = X W^K$, $V = X W^V$.
Dimensionally, $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times D}$, $W^Q, W^K \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times d}$, and $W^V \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times d'}$ with $d'$ typically equal to $d$.
The matrix of all dot products is $Q K^T$.
The attention weights are $\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} Q K^T\right)$.
The output is $Z = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} Q K^T\right) V$.
The formula $Z = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} Q K^T\right) V$ is the main attention formula from the paper "Attention Is All You Need".
The raw affinities are dot products between vectors of length $d$.
If query and key entries are considered random with zero mean and unit variance, each dot product is a sum of $d$ such products.
The expected magnitude of such a sum after $d$ steps is on the order of $\sqrt{d}$.
Without rescaling, these large values push the softmax into regions of extreme saturation.
Dividing by $\sqrt{d}$ keeps the logits at a moderate scale.
If $d$ is 64, then adding 64 numbers gives a sum on the order of $\pm 8$.
A logit of $\pm 8$ makes the softmax output nearly a one-hot vector, which is too peaked.
The rescaling by $\sqrt{d}$ brings the variance back to roughly one, smoothing the softmax.
The main computational problem of transformers is that the attention matrix is $n \times n$, giving quadratic complexity in the input sequence length.
This quadratic complexity limits scaling without computational tricks.
A few years ago, large language models boasted context sizes of 128,000 or 512,000 tokens.
Now there are million-token context windows.
A million-token context is not trivial — the complexity grows with $10^6$ squared, not linearly.
You must invent tricks to handle large contexts, and a whole subfield addresses this.
Claude Opus has a separate model with a one-million-token context that is more expensive and complicated than the standard smaller-context Opus.
Geometrically, self-attention projects each input vector from a large space down to a smaller space in two different ways to obtain queries and keys.
Mathematically, self-attention uses a low-dimensional projection for queries and another same-dimensional projection for keys — two views of the vector set.
A third projection, possibly of a different dimension, gives the values.
This constitutes one attention head.
In practice, a transformer uses several attention heads, each with its own $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$ matrices.
Each attention head produces its own output and captures different aspects of the input.
In self-attention, every query looks at every input token, including itself. This all-pairs property is crucial.
In a recurrent network, information flows step-by-step through intermediate states.
Even with an LSTM’s memory cell and constant error carousel, a lot can change along the path.
A transformer can jump directly from any token to any other in one step, seeing the entire sequence at once.
This all-pairs property is a major advantage, but it comes at the cost of quadratic complexity.
Recurrent networks are linear in input length, while transformers are quadratic — a huge difference.
Transformers gain the ability to notice relations regardless of distance.
The use of value vectors in self-attention is fundamentally an efficiency choice that enables multi-head attention.
If the value length were equal to the input dimension, concatenating multiple heads would be inefficient and require too many weights.
The outputs of multiple attention heads are concatenated and then multiplied by a feedforward weight matrix to produce the final output of the same size as the input.
The reason for this combination is to allow stacking identical layers.
The intermediate representations in multi-head attention are substantially larger than the input.
If the input $X$ is of size $D \times L$ and each head outputs a matrix of size $d \times L$ (with $d$ smaller than $D$), then concatenating all heads yields a matrix of size $(H \cdot d) \times L$.
The concatenated matrix is multiplied by a feedforward weight matrix to mix the features, producing the final $Z$ of size $D \times L$.
The first intuition for multi-head attention is to provide variety: different heads can learn different projections, giving more expressive power.
The second intuition is efficiency: if each head's output dimension equaled the model dimension, the concatenated matrix would be too large to train.
Each attention head is a copy of the same operation with independent weight matrices.
All attention heads are processed in parallel.
The output of the multi-head attention is the matrix $Z$.
The described self-attention mechanism fully describes the self-attention layer of the encoder.
The decoder introduces masked self-attention.
The decoder introduces encoder-decoder attention.
At inference time, masked self-attention is regular self-attention applied to the current prefix.
Masking in self-attention is only relevant during training, for efficiency.
During training, instead of running the decoder separately for each target token, we run it once on the whole sequence.
A causal mask prevents the model from cheating during training.
In masked self-attention, for a token at position $t$, all attention weights to positions $\ge t$ are zeroed out.
Thus, token $t$ can only attend to positions $1$ through $t-1$.
Masked self-attention is an implementation trick that preserves causality while allowing one-pass training.
Encoder-decoder attention is how the decoder conditions on the encoder outputs.
Encoder-decoder attention requires no real modification to the self-attention mechanism.
In encoder-decoder attention, the self-attention picture stays the same; we simply incorporate the encoder's $Z$ outputs without changing the structure.
In encoder-decoder attention, the queries come from the decoder input $X$ by multiplying by $W_Q$.
The keys and values come from the encoder representations by multiplying by $W_K$ and $W_V$.
Unlike self-attention, in encoder-decoder attention $Q$, $K$, $V$ are not all produced from the same $X$.
$Q$ comes from the decoder input, and $K$ and $V$ come from the conditioning signal (encoder outputs).
In encoder-decoder attention, the attention matrix is not necessarily square because the number of queries and keys can differ.
The number of keys must match the number of values, but the number of queries can be different.
It is a common idea in transformers that queries come from one source while keys and values come from another.
This approach of queries from one source and keys/values from another dates back to the original Transformer decoder.
In a designed single-layer, single-head self-attention that outputs the matching key, the attention matrix points to the correct spot.
The attention weight matrix need not select a single token.
The attention matrix often resembles a permutation matrix, encoding pairwise relationships.
It is possible to have an attention matrix where queries attend uniformly to all tokens.
One token can attend to every token in the sequence (widely distributed attention).
Intuitively, a token is a word, but using words as tokens fails because there are too many words.
Lemmatizing everything would lose grammatical information.
Typos would explode the vocabulary if using words as tokens.
Character-level tokenization gives a vocabulary of a few hundred symbols.
Character-level tokenization makes sequences too long.
A context limit of a million tokens is very different for word tokens versus character tokens.
We need a tokenization method in between word-level and character-level.
Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is the standard tokenization solution.
BPE is unrelated to learning.
BPE is essentially Huffman coding from information theory.
BPE starts from a character vocabulary.
BPE adds a new token by merging the most frequent consecutive pair of characters (or tokens) that actually appears.
The merged pair becomes a new symbol.
In BPE, all occurrences of that pair are replaced with the new token.
In BPE, the individual characters remain in the vocabulary because they occur elsewhere.
Replacing occurrences of the merged pair reduces the length of token sequences.
This adds one token optimally (with respect to frequency).
The BPE process is repeated: recompute pair frequencies, merge the most frequent new pair.
Iterating BPE yields a compact, efficient vocabulary that balances sequence length and dictionary size.
BPE algorithm simply replaces pairs of tokens with a new token repeatedly.
BPE can be stopped at any time.
With a vocabulary capacity of 100,000, you run BPE until reaching that size.
A vocabulary capacity of 100,000 is too many for character-level and too few for word-level.
BPE first finds common word parts like "-ed" (past tense verb ending) and "-tion" (noun ending).
In BPE, common words become single tokens.
In BPE, uncommon words become multiple tokens.
Transformers' ability to attend from any token to any token in one step is their greatest strength.
A drawback of transformers is that they lose word order.
In recurrent networks, adjacent tokens are one step apart, and far tokens require many steps.
Transformers' attention matrix does not inherently care about adjacency.
Transformers are indifferent to word order.
To fix the loss of word order, positional encodings are added to the token embeddings.
Positional encodings encode where each token is in the sequence.
One-hot representation of position is possible but not desirable for positional encodings.
Ideally, positional encodings should support arithmetic so that the difference between encodings depends only on distance.
If $e_1, e_2, \ldots$ represent positions, we want $e_i - e_j$ to be similar to $e_{i+k} - e_{j+k}$.
For positions a fixed distance apart, the difference between their positional encodings should be constant across the sequence.
The original transformer used sinusoidal positional encodings.
The sinusoidal approach is based on a positional counting system, like binary numbers.
In binary numbers, the last digit oscillates 0,1,0,1; the next digit oscillates 0011 with twice the period, and so on.
A soft version of this uses sine waves of different frequencies in the encoding.
The frequencies start high and reduce, creating a positional system with desired properties.
The current popular approach for positional encoding is RoPE (rotary positional encodings).
In RoPE, the vector $x$ is split into 2D chunks (pairs of numbers).
Each 2D chunk is rotated by different angles.
The rotation uses a rotation matrix with $\cos(k\theta)$ and $\sin(k\theta)$ entries.
Positions are encoded as multiples of a base angle $\theta$.
Rotating by $k\theta$ and then $L\theta$ is equivalent to rotating by $(k+L)\theta$, giving perfect arithmetic.
In sinusoidal positional encoding, the dot product between two vectors depends only on the offset $i-j$.
Rotary encodings produce a dot product matrix with a diagonal structure where each diagonal has constant positional distance.
The $\sqrt{d}$ scaling in attention is necessary because without scaling, dot products grow large.
Without scaling, after softmax the distribution approaches one-hot, losing entropy.
Transformers transformed deep learning about ten years ago.
LSTM splits the hidden state into a long-term memory $C_t$ and a regular hidden state $h_t$.
$C_t$ stays on the highway.
The LSTM cell manipulates $C_t$ through gates.
A gate is a linear combination of inputs followed by an activation function.
The forget gate uses a logistic sigmoid to output numbers between 0 and 1.
The forget gate multiplies $C_t$ component-wise to erase selected elements.
The candidate cell state $\tilde{C}_t$ is produced from the same inputs via a linear layer with $\tanh$ activation.
$\tilde{C}_t$ generates new values to write into memory.
The input gate uses a sigmoid to decide which parts of $\tilde{C}_t$ are written into memory by addition.
The output gate uses a sigmoid to gate which parts of the updated $C_t$ pass through a $\tanh$ to produce $h_t$.
The LSTM provides a clear, interpretable program: you can delete from memory, write to it, and read from it.
The LSTM has remained remarkably successful since its final form in 2000.
The basic LSTM has eight weight matrices.
LSTM is expensive to train due to many weight matrices.
With modern compute, large LSTMs are practical.
AlphaStar used LSTMs.
Attention is a fundamental cognitive function.
Biologically, the visual system uses a foveal spotlight and saccadic movements to build an image.
Early recurrent visual attention models saved computation by glimpsing small parts of an image.
Those visual attention models are now outdated.
The key development was applying attention to encoder-decoder architectures for sequence tasks like machine translation.
In a basic encoder-decoder model, the encoder compresses the whole input sequence into a single fixed-size vector $z$.
The decoder uses $z$ to generate the output.
This basic approach fails for long sequences.
If $z$ is too small, it cannot capture enough information.
If $z$ is too large, the number of weights grows quadratically, making training infeasible.
The solution is attention: the decoder attends to different parts of the input at each step instead of using a single vector.
In the attention-based encoder-decoder model, the encoder processes the input bidirectionally and produces a sequence of context vectors $z_1, z_2, \dots, z_n$, one per input token.
At each decoding step $t$, an attention network takes the current decoder hidden state $h'_t$ and each $z_i$ and computes a score $a_i$.
The score $a_i$ is often computed via a small feedforward network.
The scores are normalized by softmax to produce a convex combination $U_t = \sum_i \alpha_i z_i$.
$U_t$ becomes the input to the decoder at step $t$.
The attention mechanism is not trained with explicit alignment labels.
The whole model is trained end-to-end on sentence pairs.
The model learns to align words correctly (e.g., high attention on the source word being translated).
Giving the network the structural ability to solve a task without direct supervision often succeeds.
The introduction of attention around 2014-2015 dramatically improved neural machine translation.
By 2016, Google Translate switched to attention-based architectures and became practically useful.
Transformers were introduced in 2017 with the paper "Attention is All You Need".
Transformers were originally proposed as a more efficient alternative to recurrent models.
Transformers proved extraordinarily general and scalable.
Transformers can be scaled to trillions of parameters and continue to improve.
This scaling property had never been seen before.

summary.text: Recurrent neural networks suffer from vanishing gradients.
In recurrent neural networks, the same weight matrix W is multiplied at every time step.
If the spectral radius of W is less than 1, gradients decay to zero.
Exploding gradients cause obvious numerical overflows.
Vanishing gradients are silent.
With vanishing gradients, the loss may still decrease because W trains on the last few steps.
With vanishing gradients, the network loses long-term memory.
With vanishing gradients, the network can no longer base predictions on early parts of a sequence.
A solution to vanishing gradients is to create a constant error carousel.
The constant error carousel is a highway where the gradient can flow unchanged without being repeatedly multiplied by weight matrices.
The constant error carousel was inspired by ResNet-style residual connections.
The constant error carousel insight was pioneered in Jürgen Schmidhuber’s group in the mid-1990s.
The LSTM was introduced in Hochreiter & Schmidhuber (1995) and Gers & Schmidhuber (2000).
The LSTM cell maintains a cell state c_t.
The cell state c_t lives on the gradient highway.
The LSTM cell maintains a hidden state h_t.
The hidden state h_t participates in the cell's operations.
Information flow in the LSTM is controlled by three gates: input, forget, and output.
Each gate is a small sub-network.
Each gate outputs a vector of values in (0,1) via the logistic sigmoid.
Each gate multiplies other vectors component-wise to erase, write, or read from memory.
The LSTM has a clear, interpretable program that allows deleting selected parts of memory, adding new values, and deciding what to expose to the output.
The candidate cell state c'_t is computed as c'_t = tanh(W_{xc} x_t + W_{hc} h_{t-1} + b_{c'}).
The input gate i_t is computed as i_t = σ(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + b_i).
The forget gate f_t is computed as f_t = σ(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + b_f).
The output gate o_t is computed as o_t = σ(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + b_o).
The cell state update is c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c'_t.
The block output is h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t).
If the forget gate f_t is fully open (f_t = 1), c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c'_t.
If f_t = 1, then the partial derivative ∂c_t/∂c_{t-1} = 1.
This allows gradients to flow unchanged, i.e., the constant error carousel property.
In the basic LSTM, the gates only see the hidden state h_{t-1} = o_{t-1} ⊙ tanh(c_{t-1}).
If the output gate is closed in the LSTM, the LSTM's behaviour becomes independent of the cell state.
Peephole connections give the gates direct access to c_{t-1}.
Peephole connections add extra weight matrices W_{pi}, W_{pf}, W_{po} to the gate equations.
The input gate with peephole is computed as i_t = σ(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + W_{pi} c_{t-1} + b_i).
The forget gate with peephole is computed as f_t = σ(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + W_{pf} c_{t-1} + b_f).
The output gate with peephole is computed as o_t = σ(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + W_{po} c_{t-1} + b_o).
The basic LSTM uses 8 weight matrices.
The basic LSTM weight matrices consist of four pairs of size d×d and d×d'.
d is typically 256–1000.
Peephole connections add three more weight matrices.
The LSTM is memory-heavy.
The LSTM is extremely effective.
The LSTM has remained the most important recurrent cell since its final form in 2000.
LSTMs are the standard in recent large-scale systems such as AlphaStar.
As of the lecture date, no alternative recurrent cell consistently outperforms the LSTM in general.
A classic toy task from Hochreiter and Schmidhuber demonstrates why gated cells are necessary.
The input has two channels: one fills a stream of random numbers, the other contains zeros except for exactly two "marker" ones.
The goal is to output the sum of the two random numbers that coincided with the markers.
A plain RNN fails completely on this task because it cannot store the first marked number long enough to add it to the second.
An LSTM learns to open its write gate exactly on the markers, store the relevant number in the cell state, and later recall it.
The running prediction of the LSTM tracks the true sum perfectly.
Gated cells are the only way to achieve this kind of long-range memory.
Many attempts have been made to simplify the LSTM while keeping the constant error carousel.
Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) were introduced by Cho et al. (2014).
GRU merges the cell state and hidden state into a single vector h_t.
GRU uses only two gates: update gate u_t and reset gate r_t.
The update gate in GRU is computed as u_t = σ(W_{xu} x_t + W_{hu} h_{t-1} + b_u).
The reset gate in GRU is computed as r_t = σ(W_{xr} x_t + W_{hr} h_{t-1} + b_r).
The candidate state in GRU is computed as h'_t = tanh(W_{xh'} x_t + W_{hh'} (r_t ⊙ h_{t-1})).
The new hidden state in GRU is h_t = (1 - u_t) ⊙ h'_t + u_t ⊙ h_{t-1}.
In GRU, erasing and writing are combined into a single convex combination driven by the update gate u_t.
The reset gate r_t determines which parts of the old memory feed into the candidate state h'_t.
GRU uses 6 weight matrices.
GRU is substantially cheaper than an LSTM.
For a fixed computational budget, GRU allows more units than LSTM.
In 2015–2016, GRUs were widely adopted in NLP.
The simple summing benchmark is solved faster by a GRU than by an LSTM.
The field later reverted to using LSTMs, e.g., AlphaStar uses LSTM.
Why the LSTM remains empirically superior on hard, large-scale tasks is not fully understood.
The superiority of LSTM illustrates that neural architecture search has not found a recurrent cell that genuinely outscores the 25-year-old LSTM across a wide range of problems.
Greff et al. (2015) showed that some drastically simplified LSTM variants perform nearly as well as the LSTM.
None of the simplified variants displace the LSTM as the default robust choice.
Attention is, in large part, an interaction with working memory (Knudsen, 2007).
In human vision, the fovea is tiny.
We only see a small, sharp snippet at any instant.
The eyes move in rapid saccades, sequentially fixating on different parts of the scene.
The brain stitches together a composite picture from these fixations.
This process can be both conscious and unconscious.
The Invisible Gorilla experiment (Simons & Chabris, 1999) is a dramatic demonstration.
In the Invisible Gorilla experiment, observers concentrating on counting basketball passes completely missed a person in a gorilla suit walking through the frame.
Even when looking directly at something, you may not process it if your attention is elsewhere.
Alexander Luria emphasised the triad of attention, memory, and cognition.
Working memory acts as a very short-term buffer.
Attention acts as a filter that selects which items are passed on for deeper processing.
Selective, limited-bandwidth processing inspired early attempts to model attention in neural networks.
A neural network might also benefit from deciding what to look at.
The original motivation for attention in neural networks was efficiency, not primarily biological plausibility.
For a large image, processing the whole thing is expensive.
You can instead take a few small glimpses, using only the pixels from those parts and ignoring or blurring the rest.
This drastically reduces the input size and thus the number of parameters and computations.
Early work by Larochelle & Hinton (2010) modelled saccades as a sequence of glimpses, learning where to look next.
The idea was fully realised in "Recurrent Models of Visual Attention" (Mnih et al., 2014).
In this model, at each step a recurrent network receives a glimpse g_t derived from the current observation and previous location.
The network updates its hidden state h_t and outputs a new location l_t and action a_t.
The glimpse is computed as g_t = f_g(x_t, l_{t-1}; θ_g).
The hidden state update is h_t = f_h(h_{t-1}, g_t; θ_h).
The location is sampled from l_t ∼ p(⋅ | f_l(h_t; θ_l)).
The action is sampled from a_t ∼ p(⋅ | f_a(h_t; θ_a)).
A reward r_t is received after the action.
The objective is correct final classification.
This defines a stochastic policy π((l_t,a_t) | s_{1:t}; θ) implemented by an RNN.
The goal is to maximise expected total reward J(θ) = E[\sum_{t=1}^T r_t].
Because the choice of location is non-differentiable, reinforcement learning (REINFORCE) is used.
Subsequent work extended this to deep variational models (Ba et al., 2015) and image generation with DRAW (Gregor et al., 2015).
Recurrent visual attention is now largely outdated.
It introduced the key idea of using a recurrent mechanism to choose where to look, which later became central in encoder-decoder architectures.
Machine translation is the canonical sequence-to-sequence problem.
A recurrent language model factors a sequence X as p(X) = p(x_1) p(x_2 | x_1) … p(x_T | x_{<T}).
In an encoder-decoder for translation, an encoder RNN compresses the source sentence into a single fixed-size vector z.
A decoder RNN generates the target sentence conditioned on z (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014).
The critical limitation is the bottleneck: everything must be squeezed through one vector.
Plotting translation quality against source sentence length reveals a sharp drop after short sentences.
Performance is excellent for short sentences, then drops catastrophically.
The cause is that a vector of manageable size cannot hold all the necessary information for long sentences.
Making the vector larger explodes the number of weights, making training infeasible.
The solution is to let the decoder attend to all encoder hidden states, weighted by relevance, instead of relying on a single summary vector.
The encoder still processes the input (bidirectionally) and produces a sequence of representations h_1, …, h_n, one per source token.
At each decoding step t, an attention network computes a score e_{tj} = a(z_{t-1}, h_j).
The attention weights are α_{tj} = softmax(e_{tj}).
The context vector is c_t = Σ_j α_{tj} h_j.
The context vector c_t is a convex combination of all encoder outputs.
The context vector c_t is fed to the decoder: z_t = f(s_{t-1}, y_{t-1}, c_t).
The network is never given explicit word-alignment labels.
Attention weights are learned purely from the translation loss.
They reliably discover which source tokens correspond to which target tokens (e.g., "world" → "mir").
The attention mechanism accounts for about 2% of the total parameters but is what separates usable translation from the cliff.
Visualising α matrices yields interpretable patterns: mostly diagonal for similar word order, off-diagonal for syntactic differences, reverse diagonals for reversal tasks.
Wu et al. (2016) scaled the encoder-decoder with attention to 8 encoder and 8 decoder layers of LSTMs.
They added residual connections to make training deeper layers feasible.
The bottom encoder layer was bidirectional.
This system powered Google Translate for several years.
Around 2015–2016, it produced a phase transition: post-editing machine translation became faster than translating from scratch.
The architecture can be used across modalities, e.g., CNN encoder + LSTM decoder for image captioning.
"Show and Tell" (Vinyals et al., 2015) simply fed a fixed image feature vector to an LSTM decoder.
"Show, Attend, and Tell" (Xu et al., 2015) introduced spatial attention over CNN feature vectors.
The CNN is stopped early, retaining a 14×14 grid of vectors a_i that preserve spatial layout.
At each decoding step a context vector is formed as a weighted sum φ({a_i},{α_{t,i}}) = Σ_i α_{t,i} a_i.
Two attention variants were studied: soft attention and hard attention.
Soft attention is a deterministic, differentiable convex combination, trained end-to-end.
Hard attention is stochastic sampling from the attention distribution, trained by maximising a variational lower bound.
The variational lower bound is L_s = Σ_s p(s | a) log p(y | s, a) ≤ log p(y | a).
The gradient of hard attention is ∂L_s/∂W = Σ_s p(s | a)[ ∂log p(y | s, a)/∂W + log p(y | s, a) ∂log p(s | a)/∂W ].
Hard attention is approximated by sampling \(s\) from the attention distribution \(\alpha_i\).
Attention maps are interpretable.

For the caption “a woman is throwing a frisbee in the park,” the model focuses on people for “woman,” on the throwing motion for “throwing,” on the disc for “frisbee,” and on the background for “park.”
Visual debugging using attention maps helps diagnose failures directly from the attention.
The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) stands as arguably the single most important architecture in modern deep learning.
The original Transformer paper was presented as a more efficient way to do sequence-to-sequence modeling.
The Transformer proved to be remarkably general, effectively discovering internal correlations in sequences of vectors regardless of their origin (text, images, etc.).
The Transformer proved to be highly scalable, with performance continuing to improve as parameters and data increase from millions to trillions of parameters, without saturating.
LSTMs never achieved such scalability; they either became untrainable or saturated much earlier.
The Transformer abandons recurrence entirely and processes all tokens in parallel.
The Transformer encoder consists of a stack of identical layers.
Each encoder layer contains a multi-head self-attention sublayer followed by a position-wise feedforward network.
Residual connections and layer normalization surround each sublayer in the encoder.
The Transformer decoder follows the same pattern as the encoder but adds masked self-attention and encoder-decoder attention.
Input tokens are first converted to dense vectors by a learnable embedding layer.
Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings to inject sequence order.
The decoder is autoregressive: it generates output tokens one by one.
The decoder conditions on both its own previously generated tokens and the final encoder representations.
The decoder uses a linear + softmax head to produce next-token probabilities.
Self-attention is directly inspired by neural information retrieval.
In neural information retrieval, queries and documents are embedded into a common latent space so that relevant pairs have high dot-product similarity.
Self-attention treats every position in a set of vectors as both a query and a document.

Given an input sequence \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times L}\), the model computes queries \(Q = W_Q X\), keys \(K = W_K X\), and values \(V = W_V X\), with weight matrices \(W_Q, W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times D}\) and \(W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_v \times D}\) (typically \(d_v = d\)).
The attention function is \(\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} Q K^{\top} \right) V\).
The matrix \(QK^\top\) contains the dot-product similarities between every query–key pair.
Scaling by \(1/\sqrt{d}\) is critical: if query and key entries behave like i.i.d. variables with zero mean and unit variance, a dot product’s expected magnitude is on the order of \(\sqrt{d}\).
Without scaling by \(1/\sqrt{d}\), the large values push the softmax into a nearly one‑hot regime (extreme saturation).
Dividing by \(\sqrt{d}\) keeps the logits at a moderate scale and the softmax smooth, enabling stable gradient flow.
In the Transformer, every position attends to every other position in a single operation.
In a recurrent network, information must travel step‑by‑step; in the Transformer a token can directly draw on any other token, regardless of distance.
The Transformer eliminates the sequential bottleneck but brings quadratic complexity in the sequence length \(L\) because the attention matrix is \(L \times L\).
Handling very long contexts (millions of tokens) requires specialized tricks to keep computation feasible.
A single attention head captures one type of relationship.
Multi‑head attention uses \(H\) independent heads, each with its own weight matrices \(W_Q^{(i)}, W_K^{(i)}, W_V^{(i)}\), producing outputs \(Z^1,\dots,Z^H\) of size \(d_v \times L\).

The head outputs are concatenated into a \((H d_v) \times L\) matrix and linearly projected back to the model dimension \(D\) via \(Z = \bigl(Z_{\text{concat}} W_O\bigr)^{\top}\) with \(W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{H d_v \times D}\).
The design separates the dimension of each head (\(d_v\)) from the model dimension \(D\), keeping the total number of parameters manageable.
If each head’s value dimension were as large as \(D\), the concatenated representation would be infeasibly large.
The multi‑head architecture gives the model a richer expressive capacity while staying practical.
Because the decoder generates tokens autoregressively, it must not see future positions.
Masked self‑attention achieves this during training: for every position \(t\), attention weights towards positions \(\ge t\) are set to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, forcing them to zero.
Masked self‑attention allows training the decoder on the whole target sequence in one forward pass while preserving causality.
Encoder‑decoder attention uses the decoder’s queries (from the partially generated output) but takes keys and values from the final encoder output.
The mechanism of encoder‑decoder attention is structurally identical to self-attention: the decoder queries retrieve information from the encoder’s representations.

The dimensions of queries and keys/values in encoder‑decoder attention need not match—the number of keys equals the encoder sequence length, while the number of queries equals the decoder prefix length.
Transformers work with subword tokens.
Using whole words leads to an unmanageably large vocabulary; using characters would make sequences far too long.
Byte‑Pair Encoding (BPE) is a data‑compression algorithm that builds a vocabulary by iteratively merging the most frequent pair of consecutive symbols.
BPE repeatedly counts adjacent pairs of tokens in the corpus, merges the most frequent pair into a new token, and replaces every occurrence of that pair with the new token.

For example, given words {cat:10, pet:12, mat:5, rat:8, eats:4}, splitting into characters yields the pair “at” with 27 occurrences; merging “at” into a new symbol \(Z\) produces {cZ:10, pet:12, mZ:5, rZ:8, eZs:4}.
The BPE merging process continues until the desired vocabulary size is reached.
In language, early BPE merges capture common morphemes like “‑ed” and “‑tion”; very common words become single tokens, while rare words are split into subword pieces.
BPE is unrelated to gradient‑based learning; it is pure data compression that yields highly efficient tokenization.
Self‑attention is completely invariant to token order—it treats the sequence as a set.
To inject position information, the Transformer adds positional encodings to the input embeddings.
The original Transformer used sinusoidal positional encodings: \(PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin(pos/10000^{2i/d})\), \(PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos(pos/10000^{2i/d})\).
This design ensures that the dot product of two sinusoidal positional encodings depends only on the offset \(pos_1 - pos_2\), enabling the model to easily recover relative distances.
Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE) is a more recent and widely adopted alternative.
RoPE breaks each token vector into pairs of coordinates and rotates each pair by an angle that is a multiple of the position index and a base frequency.

In RoPE, if the pair \((x_{2i}, x_{2i+1})\) is rotated by \(\begin{pmatrix} \cos(k\theta) & -\sin(k\theta) \\ \sin(k\theta) & \cos(k\theta) \end{pmatrix}\), then rotating by \(k\theta\) and later by \(l\theta\) yields rotation by \((k+l)\theta\), giving a clean algebraic property and smooth, distance‑dependent similarity.
RoPE is now the default positional encoding in most large language models.
The Transformer trains roughly 100× faster than comparable recurrent models and achieves superior translation quality.
Because any token can directly attend to any other, long‑range dependencies are handled much better in Transformers than in RNNs.
The attention weights themselves provide a window into what the model learns—one can visualise which tokens are attended to at each layer, revealing syntactic and semantic patterns.
The Transformer’s scalability and generality have made it the foundation of virtually all subsequent advances in language and multimodal modeling.
